passage:
Imran, sit. You want to know why I nag your Abbu about his check-ups? Let me tell you. When I was twenty-five and he was twenty-eight, he started getting dizzy at work. He'd sit on the stairs for a minute and wave it off. "It's the heat, Usha, don't make a drama." But I saw how he avoided even walking past the clinic. He was afraid of what they'd say.
Shouting didn't work; our Ammi tried that. So one Saturday I just said, "I have to go for my own blood test. Come sit with me." He came. In the waiting room I said, "Since we're here..." and he nodded.
The doctor found what it was, and it was treatable. He was lucky. I stayed with him for every appointment after that. That's why I still ask, beta.

qa.q: Where did Imran's Abbu sit when he felt dizzy at work?
qa.a: He would sit on the stairs for a minute and wave it off.

qa.q: Why did Imran's Abbu avoid even walking past the clinic?
qa.a: He was afraid of what the doctors would say, so not going kept that fear away, even though the dizziness kept happening.

qa.q: What worked better than shouting to get him to the doctor?
qa.a: Usha went along gently, asking him to come and sit through Usha's own blood test, so the visit felt like company rather than pressure, and a doctor could then look at it properly.

qa.q: How might Imran see Usha's nagging after hearing this story?
qa.a: Imran might understand it comes from love and a real scare, not fussing, and feel grateful Usha stayed with his Abbu.

grounding: It shows Usha noticing Imran's Abbu delaying a check-up out of fear, and how gentle company to the appointment and a doctor's care helped more than pressure.

passage:
Rajni had noticed it for weeks: her brother Vishal squinting at his phone, rubbing his temples after his shift, turning down the evening cricket match because the lights "hurt". When she mentioned the eye clinic, he said, "Next month," every time. Once he admitted, "What if they say something's really wrong?"
She booked the appointment herself for Saturday morning, his only free day. On Saturday it poured, the auto stand was empty, and the clinic was across the city.
Vishal looked relieved. "See, it's a sign. We'll go next month."
Rajni pulled out two raincoats. "I'll drive the scooter. I'll wait with you. Whatever they say, you won't hear it alone."
They arrived soaked and ten minutes late. The receptionist squeezed them in. In the waiting room Vishal held his raincoat on his knees and didn't say much, but he stayed.

qa.q: When did Rajni book the eye clinic appointment?
qa.a: Rajni booked it for Saturday morning, Vishal's only free day.

qa.q: Why did Vishal look relieved when it poured?
qa.a: He was afraid the doctor might say something was really wrong, so the rain gave him an excuse to delay facing it.

qa.q: What in Rajni's approach helped Vishal go?
qa.a: She didn't argue or scare him; she removed the obstacles, offered to drive and wait, and promised he wouldn't hear the news alone.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had agreed to wait until next month?
qa.a: The headaches and squinting would carry on unchecked, and Vishal's fear might grow as he kept pushing the visit away.

grounding: It shows a sister seeing her brother avoid an eye check-up out of fear and helping by gently going with him, despite bad weather.

passage:
Varun knew something was up when his younger brother Nitin started chewing only on the left side at dinner. In their Andheri flat, Nitin kept a painkiller strip in his bag and said it was just a bit of a toothache.
The first week, Varun tried pressure. "Go to the dentist. You're being a baby." Nitin slammed the door.
The second week he tried something else. At breakfast he said, "I hated the dentist too, remember my braces? I'm going for a cleaning on Thursday evening. Come with me, and if you want, they can have a look at yours too."
Nitin shrugged. On Thursday he came. In the waiting room his knee bounced the whole time. Varun didn't talk; he just sat next to him and passed him his earphones.
When Nitin's name was called, he stood up and went in.

qa.q: What did Nitin keep in his bag?
qa.a: Nitin kept a painkiller strip in his bag.

qa.q: What does Nitin's bouncing knee in the waiting room suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous and scared of what the dentist might find or do, which is likely why he had been delaying.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: The second one: Varun shared his own fear, made it a shared outing, and just sat with Nitin, which felt safe instead of shaming.

qa.q: How did Nitin probably feel when Varun called him a baby?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and defensive, which is why he slammed the door instead of agreeing to go.

grounding: It shows a brother noticing his sibling delay a dental check-up out of fear, and that gentle company to the appointment works better than pressure.

passage:
"Pranav, you've skipped dinner again."
"Not hungry, Ishita. Stomach's a bit off."
"It's been 'a bit off' since Diwali. I've seen you pressing your side on the stairs."
"It's nothing. Probably gas. If I go to a doctor, they'll find something, then tests, then..."
"So you'd rather not know?"
Pranav went quiet. "Something like that."
Ishita sat down beside her brother. "I'm not going to nag. I'll book the clinic for Saturday morning and come with you. You do the talking, I'll hold the file. If it's gas, we get chaat after."
"And if it's not?"
"Then we'll know early, and the doctor will tell us what's next. Either way, you're not going alone."
Pranav let out a breath. "Saturday. But you're buying the chaat."

qa.q: What has Ishita seen Pranav doing on the stairs?
qa.a: Pressing his side on the stairs.

qa.q: What is Pranav afraid of when he avoids the doctor?
qa.a: He fears a visit will uncover something serious and lead to tests, so not knowing feels safer for now.

qa.q: Which choice by Ishita helped Pranav agree, and why?
qa.a: Instead of nagging, Ishita booked the clinic and offered to come along and hold the file, so he didn't have to face it alone.

qa.q: How might Ishita's offer feel from Pranav's side?
qa.a: It likely felt like relief rather than pressure: someone handling the practical steps and staying beside him, so the fear felt smaller.

grounding: A sibling notices her brother avoiding a check-up out of fear and offers gentle company to the doctor instead of pressure.

passage: Last winter my older sister Kiran coughed through the nights in the room we share in Ludhiana. She'd laugh it off: "Winter throat." I tried pressure first. I forwarded her scary articles, and once I told her in front of Mummy that she was being stupid. She just coughed more quietly, into her pillow, and stopped mentioning it. That frightened me more than the cough. So one evening I changed tack. "I'm going to the clinic on Thursday for my own check-up. Come with me? Kulfi after." She was quiet, then nodded. In the waiting room she held my hand like when we were kids. The doctor listened properly and gave her a plan to follow. What helped wasn't my arguing. It was sitting beside her. I'm Baljeet, and I'm still learning that.

qa.q: What did Kiran call her cough?
qa.a: Winter throat.

qa.q: Why did Kiran start coughing more quietly into her pillow?
qa.a: The pressure made her feel judged and scared, so she hid the cough rather than face it or be argued with.

qa.q: What turning point does Baljeet describe, and why did it work?
qa.a: Inviting Kiran along to a shared clinic visit with kulfi after; gentle company felt safe, while arguing had only pushed her to hide it.

qa.q: What was that waiting room like for Kiran?
qa.a: She was probably frightened, holding Baljeet's hand like a child, but comforted not to face the doctor alone 🤍

grounding: A sibling learns that pressure made a sister hide her symptoms, while gentle company to the clinic and a doctor's advice helped.
